policies.profileSelection: Non-rejected claims with at least one approved credible source may appear in the Mentor-review draft. Their original review status and approval origin remain explicit.
policies.factualSourcing: Every selected statement has at least one approved institutional, primary-text, or scholarly source.
policies.contestedMaterial: Contested or sensitive statements require two independent approved credible sources and at least one primary-text or scholarly source; failures are withheld and reported.
policies.mentorSignOff: Per the Track 2 handoff, Track 1 profiles, presentation mapping, framework, sourcing decisions, portable dataset, schema, and SOP are approved for the Phase 1 demo. No Mentor identity, signature, or date is invented by this export.

shortIntroduction.text: As project director, Kalam led development of India's first indigenous satellite launch vehicle, SLV-III, which put Rohini into near-Earth orbit in July 1980.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: Kalam made significant contribution as Project Director to develop India's first indigenous Satellite Launch Vehicle (SLV-III) which successfully injected the Rohini satellite in the near earth orbit in July 1980 and made India an exclusive member of Space Club.

shortIntroduction.text: Kalam served as India's eleventh president from 25 July 2002 to 25 July 2007.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: Kalam became the 11th President of India on 25th July 2002. His focus is on transforming India into a developed nation by 2020.

lifeAndContext.text: As project director, Kalam led development of India's first indigenous satellite launch vehicle, SLV-III, which put Rohini into near-Earth orbit in July 1980.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: Kalam made significant contribution as Project Director to develop India's first indigenous Satellite Launch Vehicle (SLV-III) which successfully injected the Rohini satellite in the near earth orbit in July 1980 and made India an exclusive member of Space Club.

lifeAndContext.text: Kalam served as India's eleventh president from 25 July 2002 to 25 July 2007.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: Kalam became the 11th President of India on 25th July 2002. His focus is on transforming India into a developed nation by 2020.

lifeAndContext.text: Kalam was born in Rameswaram, Tamil Nadu, in 1931 and trained in aeronautical engineering at Madras Institute of Technology.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: Abdul Kalam Download Profile PhotoBorn on 15th October 1931 at Rameswaram in Tamil Nadu, Dr. Avul Pakir Jainulabdeen Abdul Kalam, specialized in Aeronautical Engineering from Madras Institute of Technology.

lifeAndContext.text: The government's memorial account credits Kalam with leadership in the development and operationalisation of the Agni and Prithvi missile systems.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: Kalam was responsible for the development and operationalisation of AGNI and PRITHVI Missiles. He gave thrust to self-reliance in defence systems by introducing Light Combat Aircraft.

qualitiesValues.text: He envisaged narrowing the rural–urban divide and improving access to water, energy, and education as measures of national development.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: A Nation where the rural and urban divide has reduced to a thin line, by establishing 7,000 rural clusters and providing urban facilities in them.2.

qualitiesValues.text: In India 2020, Kalam and Rajan linked scientific and technological strength with poverty reduction, health, education, and economic opportunity.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: However, the vision of a prosperous India without poverty, an India strong in trade and commerce, an India strong in many fields of science and technology, an India with innovative industry and with health and education for all, has remained just partially realized. In some areas, in fact, pessimism has taken deep roots.We have completed the fiftieth year of our independence, with a large majority born after independence.

qualitiesValues.text: Kalam used Dhawan's response to SLV failure and success as a model of leaders taking responsibility for setbacks and sharing credit for success.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: And also, I gratefully remember the second scene, when I and my team succeeded in launching the Second SLV3; he gave the whole credit to me and my team. Through this experience, I learnt how to defeat the problems and also the leadership quality to manage the failures.

qualitiesValues.text: Kalam's development agenda combined agriculture and food processing, education and healthcare, ICT, infrastructure, and strategic technological self-reliance.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: We have identified five areas where India has core competencies for integrated action: (1) Agriculture and Food processing (2) Education and Healthcare (3) Information and Communication Technology (4) Infrastructure: Reliable and Quality Electric power, Transportation system and related Infrastructure for all parts of the country including providing urban facilities and basic necessities in rural clusters.

contributions.text: The July 1980 SLV-3 launch placed Rohini RS-1 in orbit and established an indigenous Indian satellite-launch capability.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: SLV-3 was successfully launched on July 18, 1980 from Sriharikota Range (SHAR), when Rohini satellite, RS-1, was placed in orbit, thereby making India the sixth member of an exclusive club of space-faring nations .

contributions.text: The presidential profile credits Kalam with helping shape the later Indian launch vehicle programme, especially the PSLV configuration.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: He was responsible for the evolution of ISRO's launch vehicle programme, particularly the PSLV configuration. After working for two decades in ISRO and mastering launch vehicle technologies, Dr.

contributions.text: The SLV-3 programme developed a four-stage solid-propellant launch vehicle able to place small payloads in low Earth orbit.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: LV Home / Activities / Missions accomplished Satellite Launch Vehicle-3 (SLV-3) was India's first experimental satellite launch vehicle, which was an all solid, four stage vehicle weighing 17 tonnes with a height of 22m and capable of placing 40 kg class payloads in Low Earth Orbit (LEO (Low Earth Orbit) ).

contributions.text: Kalam advocated PURA, or Providing Urban Amenities in Rural Areas, as a development model for village clusters.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: This will provide direct quality employment to over one million who will be instrumental in promoting higher level of wealth generation in PURA Complexes.ConclusionAs you are aware we have been talking about PURA (Providing Urban Amenities in Rural Areas) as a growth driver of our economy for the last few years. Also number of conferences has been held by different institutions for conceptualization and implementation of PURA.

contributions.text: Kalam described education as learning from teachers, libraries, and laboratories, a view that joined classroom knowledge with practical inquiry.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: Our education is what we learn in the class and from teachers, what we learn in the Libraries and what we learn in the laboratories. I received an excellent education at my School at Schwartz High School, Ramanathapuram and later at St Joseph's College, Tiruchirapalli.

contributions.text: Kalam's PURA proposal joined physical, electronic, and knowledge connectivity to expand rural economic opportunity.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: This PURA complex has all the three Connectivities - physical, electronic and knowledge - leading to economic connectivity. The center of activity emanates from the women engineering college that provides the electronic and knowledge connectivity.

challenges.text: The first experimental SLV-3 flight in August 1979 was only partially successful; the programme reached orbit on its next attempt in July 1980.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: The first experimental flight of SLV-3, in August 1979, was only partially successful. Apart from the July 1980 launch, there were two more launches held in May 1981 and April 1983, orbiting Rohini satellites carrying remote sensing sensors.

challenges.text: Kalam recalled missing selection as an Air Force pilot and moving into technical work in aerospace and defence instead.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: Even though, I couldn't get into Air force as a pilot, I started my carrier as a technical assistant. phase1PresentationCategory.name: Sages & Philosophical Traditions
phase1PresentationCategory.description: Seers and philosophers whose teachings, texts, and traditions shaped enduring ideas about knowledge, discipline, and spiritual life.

shortIntroduction.text: Shankara is securely described as an influential early Advaita Vedanta philosopher, commonly placed in the eighth century, while exact dates and most biographical details remain disputed.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: The fundamental thrust of Advaita Vedanta is that the atman is pure non-intentional consciousness. It is one without a second, nondual, infinite existence, and numerically identical with brahman. This effort entails tying a metaphysics of brahman to a philosophy of consciousness. This philosophical tradition finds its most sustained early articulation in the works of the preeminent Advaita Vedantin, Sankaracarya (hereafter Sankara), who flourished during the eighth century CE. Sankara endeavored to communicate nonduality through systematized theories of metaphysics, language, and epistemology. He also incorporated specific methods of philosophical teaching, along with learning methods of listening, reflection, and contemplation. His philosophy and methods comprise a teaching tradition intended to culminate in a direct liberating recognition of nonduality that is synonymous with liberation or freedom (moksa).

shortIntroduction.text: Advaita Vedanta predates Shankara: he systematized and powerfully defended an already existing nondual current rather than creating nonduality from nothing.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: Vedanta is nominally a school of Indian philosophy, although in reality it is a label for any hermeneutics that attempts to provide a consistent interpretation of the philosophy of the Upanisads or, more formally, the canonical summary of the Upanisads, Badarayana’s Brahma Sutra. Advaita is often translated as “non-dualism” though it literally means “non-secondness.” Although Sankara is regarded as the promoter of Advaita Vedanta as a distinct school of Indian philosophy, the origins of this school predate Sankara. The existence of an Advaita tradition is acknowledged by Sankara in his commentaries. The names of Upansadic teachers such as Yajnavalkya, Uddalaka, and Badarayana, the author of the Brahma Sutra, could be considered as representing the thoughts of early Advaita.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: The school divides the Vedas into two sections: karmakanda, the section of spiritual exegesis (consisting of the Samhitas and the Brahmanas), and jnanakanda, the section of knowledge (consisting of the Upanisads, and to a certain extent, the Aranyakas). According to the Vedanta school, the ritual section contains detailed instructions of how to perform the rituals, whereas the Upanisads contain transcendent knowledge for the sake of achieving moksa. There are three main branches of the Vedanta school: Advaita Vedanta, Visistadvaita Vedanta, and Dvaita Vedanta. Although these branches would put forth distinct philosophical positions, they all took sabda as the exclusive means to knowledge about its central doctrines and considered the Upanisads, the Brahma Sutra, and Bhagavad Gita as its core texts (prasthanatraya).

lifeAndContext.text: Mandana Misra represents an important near-contemporary Advaita-related interlocutor: he gave greater weight than Shankara to combining knowledge and action on the path to liberation.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: Sankara is supposed to have had four (prominent) pupils: Padmapada, Suresvara, Hastamalaka and Totaka. Padmapada is said to be his earliest student. Panchapadika, by Padmapada, is a lucid commentary on Sankara’s commentary on the first verses of the Brahma Sutra. Suresvara is supposed to have written Naiskarmya Siddhi, an independent treatise on Advaita. Mandana Misra (eight century), an earlier adherent of the rival school of Bhatta Mimamsa, is responsible for a version of Advaita which focuses on the doctrine of sphota, a semantic theory held by the Indian philosopher of language Bhartrhari. He also accepts to a greater extent the joint importance of knowledge and works as a means to liberation, when for Sankara knowledge is the one and only means.

challenges.text: The Advaita discipline associated with Shankara includes discrimination between permanent and impermanent, dispassion, mental and ethical disciplines, and a desire for liberation.

citations.locator: IEP: Error, True Knowledge and Practical Teachings
citations.evidenceExcerpt: On the basis of his theory of knowledge, Sankara elucidates the fourfold (mental and physical) practices or qualifications—sadana catustaya—to aid in the achievement of liberation: (i) the discrimination (viveka) between the permanent (nitya) and the impermanent (anitya) objects of experience; (ii) dispassion towards the enjoyment of fruits of action here and in heaven; (iii) accomplishment of means of discipline such as calmness, mental control etc.; (iv) a longing for liberation. In his commentary to theBrahma Sutra, Sankara says that the inquiry into Brahman could start only after acquiring these fourfold qualifications. The concept of liberation (moksa) in Advaita is cashed out in terms of Brahman. The pathways to liberations are defined by the removal of self-ignorance that is brought about by the removal of mithyajnana (erroneous knowledge claims). This is captured in the formula of one Advaitin: “[He] is never born again who knows that he is the only one in all beings like the ether and that all beings are in him” (Upadesa Sahasri XVII.69).

leadershipRelationalCharacteristics.text: Accounts of Shankara’s all-India digvijaya, public victories in debate, and detailed monastic foundations are transmitted chiefly through later hagiographical and institutional traditions.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: There are no dependable historical records of Sankara’s life beyond his written works which provide few biographical clues. Scholars are also not clear about his religious identity. According to the Advaita Vedanta tradition itself, he was Saiva (a devotee of the deity Siva); but several scholars believe he was Vaisnava, a devotee of the deity Visnu (see Clark 2006: 159–170 for an overview of these theories). Hagiographical accounts of his life, the Sankaravijayas (Conquests of Sankara), were composed several centuries after his death. citations.evidenceExcerpt: The fundamental thrust of Advaita Vedanta is that the atman is pure non-intentional consciousness. It is one without a second, nondual, infinite existence, and numerically identical with brahman. This effort entails tying a metaphysics of brahman to a philosophy of consciousness. This philosophical tradition finds its most sustained early articulation in the works of the preeminent Advaita Vedantin, Sankaracarya (hereafter Sankara), who flourished during the eighth century CE. Sankara endeavored to communicate nonduality through systematized theories of metaphysics, language, and epistemology. He also incorporated specific methods of philosophical teaching, along with learning methods of listening, reflection, and contemplation. His philosophy and methods comprise a teaching tradition intended to culminate in a direct liberating recognition of nonduality that is synonymous with liberation or freedom (moksa).

The concept of illusion, in Advaita Vedanta, is significant because it leads to the theory of a “real substratum.” The illusory object, like the real object, has a definite locus. According to Sankara, adhyasais not possible without a substratum. Padmapada says in Pancapadika that adhyasa without a substratum has never been experienced and is inconceivable. Vacaspati affirms that there cannot be a case of illusion where the substratum is fully apprehended or not apprehended at all.

According to Sankara the fundamental teaching of the Upanisads is that atman and brahman are one and the same. For Sankara, the Upanisads are not merely sources to back up his claims, but they also provide him with techniques for making his arguments. citations.evidenceExcerpt: The school divides the Vedas into two sections: karmakanda, the section of spiritual exegesis (consisting of the Samhitas and the Brahmanas), and jnanakanda, the section of knowledge (consisting of the Upanisads, and to a certain extent, the Aranyakas). According to the Vedanta school, the ritual section contains detailed instructions of how to perform the rituals, whereas the Upanisads contain transcendent knowledge for the sake of achieving moksa. There are three main branches of the Vedanta school: Advaita Vedanta, Visistadvaita Vedanta, and Dvaita Vedanta. Although these branches would put forth distinct philosophical positions, they all took sabda as the exclusive means to knowledge about its central doctrines and considered the Upanisads, the Brahma Sutra, and Bhagavad Gita as its core texts (prasthanatraya).

citations.evidenceExcerpt: Bhedabheda According to the Bhedabheda view, Brahman converts itself into the created, but yet maintains a distinct identity. Thus, the school holds that Brahman is both different (bheda) and not different (abheda) from creation and the individual jiva. The philosophical persuasion that has produced the most commentaries on the Brahma Sutra is the Bhedabheda philosophy. Textual evidence suggests that all of the commentaries authored prior to Sankara’s famous Advaita commentary on the Brahma Sutra subscribed to a form of Bhedabheda, which one historian calls “Pantheistic Realism” (Sharma, pp. 15-7). And on natural readings, it appears that most of the remaining commentators (but for the three famous commentators) also promulgate an interpretation of the Brahma Sutra that falls within the Bhedabheda camp.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: The fundamental thrust of Advaita Vedanta is that the atman is pure non-intentional consciousness. It is one without a second, nondual, infinite existence, and numerically identical with brahman. This effort entails tying a metaphysics of brahman to a philosophy of consciousness. This philosophical tradition finds its most sustained early articulation in the works of the preeminent Advaita Vedantin, Sankaracarya (hereafter Sankara), who flourished during the eighth century CE. Sankara endeavored to communicate nonduality through systematized theories of metaphysics, language, and epistemology. He also incorporated specific methods of philosophical teaching, along with learning methods of listening, reflection, and contemplation. His philosophy and methods comprise a teaching tradition intended to culminate in a direct liberating recognition of nonduality that is synonymous with liberation or freedom (moksa).

citations.evidenceExcerpt: This lively and difficult poetry marks Agastya as one of the great masters of the Rgvedic tradition. He is best known for three hymns, 165, 170, and 171, which together describe how Indra and the Maruts argued over a sacrifice offered by Agastya and were finally reconciled with one another, and for his dialogue with Lopamudra (179), which turns on the tension between the ascetic ideal and the responsibility to continue the family lineage. Both the set of Indra and Marut hymns and the dialogue with Lopamudra also concern questions of ritual innovation.

sourcingStandardViolationsWithheld.text: What was unusual in Ashoka’s time was not that an empire used moral language, but that a ruling monarch publicly memorialized the harm of a conquest and made dhamma a recurring imperial policy language in surviving inscriptions.
Ashoka’s inscriptions support both broad concern for religious groups and specific Buddhist commitments; historians debate how far this amounts to a “Buddhist state.”.
The surviving Ashokan corpus is crucial evidence for the early history of writing in South Asia; its Brahmi and Kharosthi inscriptions also make empire visible across varied regions.
Ashokan inscriptions in Greek and Aramaic demonstrate communication to multilingual northwestern audiences and the empire’s engagement with wider Hellenistic worlds.
Later Buddhist chronicles and legends are important evidence for Ashoka’s Buddhist memory, but they are not direct proof of events in his reign unless independently corroborated.
Claims about Buddhist councils, mass conversions or overseas missions often derive from later traditions; their historical status should be stated separately from contemporary inscriptional evidence.
Scholars caution that post-Kalinga moral language does not prove Ashoka renounced all state coercion, military capacity or frontier rule.
A credible history of Ashoka must compare inscriptions with archaeology, later textual traditions and modern reconstruction rather than collapsing those source types.
Modern knowledge of historical Ashoka changed fundamentally after nineteenth-century decipherment of Brahmi and identification of the inscriptional Piyadasi with Ashoka.
Dhamma is not safely reducible to Buddhism: its inscriptions stress ethical conduct, family obligations, non-killing, respect and administration in language meant for diverse subjects.
Identifying named Hellenistic kings helps date the diplomatic horizon of Rock Edict XIII, but the practical mechanisms and results of any missions remain uncertain.
Ashoka’s edicts are primary evidence for what the court chose to proclaim; they are not complete records of everyday governance, popular reception or every event of the reign.

sourcingStandardViolationsWithheld.text: Famous sayings attributed to Bhagat Singh should not be stored as direct quotations without reliable textual evidence; his dated prison essays offer firmer grounding than quote-site circulation.
The accused said the bombs were not intended to kill and had been thrown in empty spaces; this is their political and legal self-explanation, to be distinguished from independent reconstruction.
National Archives of India catalogues trial papers for the 1929 Assembly Bomb Case involving Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt.
National Archives holdings include Lahore Conspiracy Case material, providing a route to colonial legal records beyond later popular retellings.

Scholars caution that Bhagat Singh should not be treated as Gandhi’s simple violent opposite: they shared an anti-colonial field but differed sharply over force, suffering, strategy and political ethics.
The Gandhi–Bhagat Singh comparison is most useful when it avoids caricature: nonviolence, revolutionary violence, mass politics and moral performance interacted in late colonial India.
Visual commemoration has often detached Bhagat Singh’s image from the complexity of his organizations, reading and political development.
Jallianwala Bagh and Punjab repression were formative public contexts, but the popular story that one childhood visit mechanically produced Bhagat Singh’s later politics is biographically too simple.
Why I Am an Atheist is strong evidence for Bhagat Singh’s late prison position, but it should not be used to erase changes or complexity in his earlier thought.
The Assembly bombing and the Lahore Conspiracy Case can be read as political confrontations with colonial law as well as criminal proceedings, while the court record remains essential evidence.
The later circulation of Bhagat Singh’s image on posters, stickers and placards is evidence of an evolving public memory, not a substitute for his writings.
Surviving trial and prison records make it possible to distinguish colonial documentation from revolutionary self-description and later biographical accounts.
Reading Bhagat Singh’s politics alongside satyagraha does not erase the HSRA’s use of force or Gandhi’s principled nonviolence; it preserves the real disagreement.

sourcingStandardViolationsWithheld.text: The near-contemporary Sabhasad chronicle presents the coronation as a response to Shivaji's military success and the need for recognized royal status; this is courtly testimony.
The coronation tradition claimed a Sisodia Rajput descent to establish Kshatriya standing; the genealogical claim should not be treated as independently established fact.
An English embassy from Bombay left a near-contemporary account of the Raigad coronation; it is an external observer's report, not a complete account of the ceremony.
Modern Hindu nationalist uses of Shivaji belong to his later political reception and must be distinguished from evidence about his own rule.
Laine argues that a teller's historical context shapes depictions of Shivaji and Hindu-Muslim relations.
The maritime historian cautions that seventeenth-century Maratha naval power was a network of commanders, obligations, and revenue arrangements, not simply a modern standing navy.
Laine studies the Shivaji legend as a changing set of narratives rather than as a transparent record of seventeenth-century events.
Gordon's history bases its account of the Maratha state on administrative records, family papers, and historical narratives, illustrating the need to compare source types.
Historian Stewart Gordon says his Shivaji narrative prioritizes incidents corroborated by at least two reliable bakhars or by outside sources.

lifeAndContext.text: Mann notes Puratan evidence of an early Sikh self-understanding as not simply following surrounding religious practice.

citations.locator: Sikhs in their religious life did not follow
citations.evidenceExcerpt: Given this description, his home would have been a sizable establishment large enough to accommodate congregational prayers, provide facilities for the making and serving of the food, and put up visitors.24 The Puratan refers to the recitation of Guru Nanak’s Alahanhia (songs of death) and Sohila (praise) at the time of his death (Sakhi 57).25 There is also the firm belief that the Sikhs in their religious life did not follow what others around them practiced (Sakhi 41). In no uncertain terms, the Puratan reports that Kartarpur with the Guru’s dargah at its center represented the sacred site for the Sikhs.26 The presence of the Guru sanctified it, his abode served as the meeting place, and there is an expectation that the Sikhs living in distant places should make a pilgrimage, have an audience with the Guru, and meet their fellow Sikhs living there.

lifeAndContext.text: Mann reports that the Puratan Janamsakhi narrates four long journeys after Kartarpur; this is evidence of the Puratan tradition’s itinerary, not a standalone verification of each journey.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: After the establishment of Kartarpur, the Puratan reports four long missionary journeys—to the region of Sindh in the south, the Himalayan foothills in the north, Mecca in the west, and the present-day Peshawar area in the northwest.27 During these travels, the Guru is reported to have initiated people into the Sikh fold through the use of the ceremony called the “nectar of the feet” (charanamrit), organized Sikh congregations in distant places, and assigned manjis (“cots,” positions of authority) to local Sikhs, who were given authority to oversee the daily routine of their congregations.

qualitiesValues.text: In the Mūl Mantra, Ik Oankar expresses the affirmation of the One; English paraphrases are interpretive renderings of a compact Punjabi/Gurmukhi formula.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: The English paraphrase, given the inherent inadequacies of the genre translation, would read, "God is one; call Him Eternal truth; He is the Supreme creator; He knows no fear and is at enmity with none. His being is Timeless and Formless; He is autogenous, attainable through the grace of the Gurū." Its placing at the beginning of the Sikh Scripture and its use, in its entirety or in part, at a number of places in the text, especially at the opening of new rāga sections indicates the importance in the Sikh tradition of the vision that the Māl Mantra summons.

qualitiesValues.text: Japji asks how falsehood is overcome and answers by walking in accord with hukam; the cited formulation is an attributed scriptural teaching rather than a neutral historical report.

In the penultimate line of the stanza, Gurū Nānak puts the fundamental question of how enlightenment is to be gained:

citations.evidenceExcerpt: The Goindval Pothis compiled in the early 1570s refer to Guru Nanak as the “Bedi King,” who supports both the religious and the temporal dimensions of the world (Baba Nanak Vedi Patisahu din dunia ki tek, Pinjore, folio 215), and call him and his successors as the “True Kings” (Baba Nanaku, Angad, Amardas, Sache Patisah, Jalandhar, folio 8).54 The bards at the Sikh court of the subsequent decades categorized the activity of Guru Nanak in the areas of politics (raj) and spirituality (jog), and presented his line of successors as a divinely sanctioned royal dynasty (Sri guru raj abichalu atalu ad purakhi furmaio, the Bhatts, GG, 1390).55 In his vars, Bhai Gurdas presented the establishment of the Kartarpur community in terms of the minting a new coin (Maria sika jagati vich, Nanak Nirmal Panthu chalia, 1: 45). As mentioned earlier, the Guru enjoyed the supreme authority at Kartarpur; the manjis represented this in distant congregations, and the pothi containing his compositions marked a symbolic version of it.

sourcingStandardViolationsWithheld.text: The Punjabi University entry warns that terms such as command, will, or pleasure overlap with hukam but do not fully capture Guru Nanak’s technical usage.
Janamsakhis are traditional narrative life-stories of Guru Nanak, normally organized as anecdotal episodes.
Several Janamsakhi traditions developed and expanded in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, combining narrative and interpretive discourse.
The Janamsakhi entry explains that anecdotes circulated orally and were later collected in written forms, a history that cautions against treating every episode as independent documentary proof.
The reference entry says no extant Janamsakhi can be dated earlier than the mid-seventeenth century, though it allows that a nucleus developed earlier.
The Janamsakhi corpus contains distinct textual traditions, including the Miharbān tradition, and their forms and theological emphases differ.
The historiography entry states that Janamsakhis interweave oral tradition, myth, legend, and allegory and do not consistently distinguish fact from fiction.
The same reference work treats Janamsakhis as exceptionally valuable evidence for early Sikh religious memory even where they are not straightforward event records.
The historiography entry commonly places the Adi Sakhian and Puratan traditions in the late sixteenth century, with other major Janamsakhi traditions later.
For historical questions about travel, miracles, and encounters, the corpus should distinguish Janamsakhi memory from contemporaneous documentation and from later institutional teaching.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: After the establishment of Kartarpur, the Puratan reports four long missionary journeys—to the region of Sindh in the south, the Himalayan foothills in the north, Mecca in the west, and the present-day Peshawar area in the northwest.27 During these travels, the Guru is reported to have initiated people into the Sikh fold through the use of the ceremony called the “nectar of the feet” (charanamrit), organized Sikh congregations in distant places, and assigned manjis (“cots,” positions of authority) to local Sikhs, who were given authority to oversee the daily routine of their congregations.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: The Goindval Pothis compiled in the early 1570s refer to Guru Nanak as the “Bedi King,” who supports both the religious and the temporal dimensions of the world (Baba Nanak Vedi Patisahu din dunia ki tek, Pinjore, folio 215), and call him and his successors as the “True Kings” (Baba Nanaku, Angad, Amardas, Sache Patisah, Jalandhar, folio 8).54 The bards at the Sikh court of the subsequent decades categorized the activity of Guru Nanak in the areas of politics (raj) and spirituality (jog), and presented his line of successors as a divinely sanctioned royal dynasty (Sri guru raj abichalu atalu ad purakhi furmaio, the Bhatts, GG, 1390).55 In his vars, Bhai Gurdas presented the establishment of the Kartarpur community in terms of the minting a new coin (Maria sika jagati vich, Nanak Nirmal Panthu chalia, 1: 45).

sourcingStandardViolationsWithheld.text: Bose’s documented work was pioneering microwave physics and instrumentation; it should be distinguished from the separate development and commercialization of wireless telegraphy.

Claims that Bose simply “invented radio” erase the different contributions of Hertz, Lodge, Bose, Marconi, and others to electromagnetic theory, experiment, detection, signaling systems, and commercialization.
Bose’s broad living/non-living analogy is historically significant but is not equivalent to modern physiological theory.
Bose compared plant responses with animal tissues, but his analogies require separation from claims that plants possess animal-like nervous systems.
Bose used the language of nerves and reflexes by analogy with animals; that terminology reflects his theoretical program rather than modern plant anatomy.
The claim that later work confirmed most of Bose’s observations is the judgment of a modern review and should not be generalized into endorsement of every original interpretation.
Modern plant signaling research recognizes electrical processes without treating plants as possessing animal neurons, brains, or a directly homologous nervous system.
Bose’s broader claims about plant intelligence, learning, and memory drew criticism from scientists who judged the evidence insufficient.
The Royal Society archive includes a referee report on Bose’s paper “Transmission of death excitation in plants,” showing that controversial terminology entered formal scientific review.
Royal Society catalogue records establish the existence of review documents, not the scientific correctness of Bose’s conclusions.

contributions.text: At the 1963 Edinburgh International Festival she gave two Carnatic recitals, placing a major Indian vocal tradition before an international festival audience.

shortIntroduction.text: Britannica describes the Brahmo Samaj as a theistic movement within Hinduism founded in Calcutta in 1828 by Ram Mohun Roy that does not accept the authority of the Vedas or belief in avatars; the Order's biography agrees on the 1828 founding.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: The Editors of Encyclopaedia Britannica Last Updated: Article History Table of Contents Category: History & Society Sanskrit: “Society of Brahma” (Show more) Brahmo also spelled: Brahma (Show more) Date: 1828 - present (Show more) Areas Of Involvement: Christianity Hinduism Islam polytheism religious syncretism (Show more) Related People: Ram Mohan Roy (Show more) See all related content → Brahmo Samaj, (Sanskrit: “Society of Brahma”) theistic movement within Hinduism, founded in Calcutta [now Kolkata] in 1828 by Ram Mohun Roy. The Brahmo Samaj does not accept the authority of the Vedas, has no faith in avatars (incarnations), and does not insist on belief in karma (causal effects of past deeds) or samsara (the process of death and rebirth).

citations.locator: The Brahmo Samaj, which he founded in 1828
citations.evidenceExcerpt: But he always went back to the Vedas for his spiritual inspiration. The Brahmo Samaj, which he founded in 1828, was dedicated to the "worship and adoration of the Eternal, the Unsearchable, the Immutable Being, who is the Author and Preserver of the Universe". The Samaj was open to all without distinction of colour, creed, caste, nation, or religion.

shortIntroduction.text: Scholars call Vivekananda's Practical Vedanta a creative transformation of Ramakrishna's teaching, and some argue that his neo-Vedanta also reflects Western reconstructions of Advaita and Brahmo influence.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: Scholars debate whether Ramakrishna viewed himself as a Vedāntin; the case can be made that his nondualism was more Tantric than Vedāntic. What is clear is that Vivekananda's Practical Vedānta represents a creative transformation of Ramakrishna's teaching. Some argue that the officially sanctioned neo-Vedānta of the Ramakrishna movement reflects the impact upon Vivekananda of Western reconstructions of Advaita Vedānta as found in influential writers like Arthur Schopenhauer and Paul Deussen.

Among other things, this allowed Neevel to interpret Ramakrishna's concern with worldly activity as arising from his understanding of the Mother's playful śakti. This, in turn, seemed to accord better with the ideals of service that are so characteristic of the Ramakrishna Mission, since the renunciatory ethic of Advaita Vedānta less readily supports the value of worldly activity.The problem remains vexing, however, precisely because Ramakrishna's commitment to asceticism sits somewhat uncomfortably with the later ethic of social engagement promulgated by the Ramakrishna Mission. The Kathāmṛta provides numerous examples of Ramakrishna's outspoken impatience with those who spend their time trying to improve the world.

lifeAndContext.text: The Brahmo leader Pratap Chandra Mozoomdar, an admirer, wrote to Max Müller in 1895 that Ramakrishna knew no Sanskrit and perhaps not enough Bengali, attributing his wisdom to "genius and practical observation"; Müller found the judgement impartial, and the Order's biography likewise says he hardly knew how to write his name.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: For all that, he was, as you say, a real Mahatman, and I would not with- draw a single word I wrote in his praise. Ramakr/shna was not in the least a Vedantist, except that every Hindu uncon- sciously imbibes from the atmosphere around some amount of Vedantism, which is the philosophical backbone of every national cult He did not know a word of Sanskrit, and it is doubtful whether he knew enough Bengali. His spiritual wisdom was the result of genius and practical observation.' There is a ring of truth and impartiality about this, and there is no sign of jealousy, which often breaks out, even in India, among religious reformers and their followers.

citations.locator: Sri Ramakrishna had a horror of lecturing and hardly knew how to write his own name
citations.evidenceExcerpt: Keshab, on the other hand, regarded image worship as idolatry and gave allegorical explanations of the Hindu deities. Keshab was an orator and a writer of books and magazine articles; Sri Ramakrishna had a horror of lecturing and hardly knew how to write his own name, Keshab's fame spread far and wide, even reaching the distant shores of England; the Master still led a secluded life in the village of Dakshineswar. Keshab emphasized social reforms for India's regeneration; to Sri Ramakrishna God-realization was the only goal of life.

lifeAndContext.text: The Ramakrishna Order's biography says Gadadhar, later Ramakrishna, was born on 18 February 1836 at Kamarpukur, a village in Hooghly district, Bengal, to a devout brahmin family.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: Upon his return the husband found that she had conceived. It was on February 18, 1836, that the child, to be known afterwards as Ramakrishna, was born. In memory of the dream at Gaya he was given the name of Gadadhar, the "Bearer of the Mace", an epithet of Vishnu.

People Philosophy and Religion Hinduism: Biographies Ramakrishna Ramakrishna gale views updated May 17 2018 RAMAKRISHNARAMAKRISHNA (1834/6–1886) was a Hindu ecstatic and mystic, and to many Hindus a "supremely realized self" (paramahaṃsa ) and an avatāra, or incarnation of the divine. Through his disciple, Swami Vivekananda, his gospel of the truth of all religions became a source of inspiration for modern Hindu universalism.LifeBorn Gadādhar Chatterjee in an isolated village in Bengal, Ramakrishna belonged to a Vaiṣṇava brahman family whose primary deity was the avatāra of Viṣṇu, Rāma, although the family also worshiped other deities, such as Śiva and Durgā.

qualitiesValues.text: Visiting the scholar Vidyasagar on 5 August 1882, Ramakrishna is recorded saying that the Vedas, Puranas, Tantras and philosophies have been "defiled" by being spoken, while Brahman alone has not, since no one can say what it is; Vidyasagar is recorded replying that he had learnt something new.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: Only one thing has not been defiled in this way, and that is Brahman. No one has ever been able to say what Brahman is." VIDYASAGAR (to his friends): "Oh! That is a remarkable statement. I have learnt something new today." MASTER: "A man had two sons.

citations.locator: He was apprehensive and hesitant on his way to Paṇḍit Ishwarchandra Vidyāsāgar
citations.evidenceExcerpt: Also, he never knew when he would be in trance and lose control of his body and outfit.’ (LP, II: Gurubhāva-Uttarārdha, 223). He was apprehensive and hesitant on his way to Paṇḍit Ishwarchandra Vidyāsāgar’s (1820–91) home to meet him. He confided to his escort M like a child: ‘My shirt is unbuttoned.

qualitiesValues.text: Alongside his acceptance of all paths, M. records him telling a Brahmo devotee that the Eternal Religion of the rishis contains every form of worship, whereas "the modern cults" will last a few days and disappear — a reminder that his inclusiveness was framed within Hindu tradition.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: It contains all paths — the path of knowledge, the path of devotion, and so on. Other forms of religion, the modern cults, will remain for a few days and then disappear." March 23, 1884 Sri Ramakrishna was sitting in his room after his midday meal, with Rakhal, Ram, and some other devotees. He was not quite well.

qualitiesValues.text: He distinguishes the jnani, who reaches Brahman by negating the world step by step, from the vijnani, who then finds that the steps are made of the same material as the roof — that Brahman has itself become the universe and living beings.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: But the vijnani, who is more intimately acquainted with Brahman, realizes something more. He realizes that the steps are made of the same materials as the roof: bricks, lime, and brick-dust. That which is realized intuitively as Brahman, through the eliminating process of 'Not this, not this', is then found to have become the universe and all its living beings, The vijnani sees that the Reality which is nirguna, without attributes, is also saguna, with attributes.

qualitiesValues.text: In M.'s record of a conversation on 13 August 1882, Ramakrishna says God can be realized through all paths and that all religions are true, comparing the paths to stone stairs, wooden stairs, bamboo steps or a rope by which one reaches the same roof.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: I am a mere machine. (To Kedar and the other devotees) "God can be realized through all paths. All religions are true.

contributions.text: Max Müller's 1898 book on Ramakrishna drew on a written account that he asked Vivekananda, one of Ramakrishna's "most eminent pupils", to supply; the Encyclopedia of Religion lists the book as an early account by a Westerner.

But Kripal's conclusions were different, because Ramakrishna is worshiped by devotees in both India and the West, because he is regarded as a great holy man by spiritual seekers of all kinds, thanks to the chain of centers established in his name by his chief disciple, Swami Vivekananda, and by illustrious Western devotees like Christopher Isherwood, and, finally, because much of India still harbors Victorian attitudes toward sexuality, especially of the same-sex variety.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: In the furor over the book two things were overlooked. First, far from trying to stigmatize Ramakrishna's sexuality, Kripal sought to recognize it as one dimension of a profoundly spiritual life; second, Kripal explicitly rejected any simplistic psychologism that reduced Ramakrishna's spirituality to a matter of pathology. Unflattering psycho-biographies of Ramakrishna exist, but they seem to have attracted far less attention than Kālī's Child, which suggests the degree to which the task of interpreting Ramakrishna must include reflection upon the place of Hinduism, Tantra, and the erotic in modern discourse about India.

sourcingStandardViolationsWithheld.text: Walter Neevel (1976), building on Heinrich Zimmer, argued that Ramakrishna's view of the ultimate is best understood as Tantric nondualism rather than Vedantic, which fits his concern with worldly activity as the Mother's playful power.

Scholars suggest Victorian-era stigma attached to Tantra made Vivekananda and the early disciples sensitive about foregrounding it, and that "bourgeois prudery" among devotees and Western interpreters led to aspects of his psychosexual life being denied or interpreted away.

Scholars say the Ramakrishna Mission's official position treats his experience as epitomised by Advaita Vedanta, relativising his Tantric transformation under Yogeshvari beneath Totapuri's teaching, and they ask why Tantra is played down in the official literature.

Writing as a historian, Sil insists that "academic history can never be hagiography", which the faithful, he says, treat as fact; he defends reasonable scholarly speculation made with explicit qualifiers.

The Order's biography claims he was "the first religious prophet recorded in history" to preach the harmony of religions, yet its own account says Keshab Sen was discovering the harmony of religions around the time of their first contact — a superlative best read as devotional reception, not history.

The reception of Kali's Child split: in India attempts were made to ban it and Kripal was threatened, while most US scholars of religion praised it; a Vedanta Society reviewer likewise reports calls for the Indian government to ban it.
Max Müller quotes Mozoomdar crediting Ramakrishna with developing Keshab Chunder Sen's idea of the Motherhood of God, and leaves open whether Keshab's later mystic turn was inspired by him.

Müller warned that even Vivekananda's account of his master shows the "Dialogic Process" of legend-making: veneration makes it natural to omit anything unfavourable, and doubt is treated as unkindness — a contemporary reminder to separate testimony from history.

Perhaps born in the Punjab, he was the head of a monastery in that province of India and claimed leadership of seven hundred sannyasis. Trained from early youth in the disciplines of the Advaita Vedanta, he looked upon the world as an illusion. The gods and goddesses of the dualistic worship were to him mere fantasies of the deluded mind. Exercising self-exertion and unshakable will-power, he had liberated himself from attachment to the sense-objects of the relative universe. For forty years he had practised austere discipline on the bank of the sacred Narmada and had finally realized his identity with the Absolute. citations.evidenceExcerpt: Eight years later, some time in November 1874, Sri Ramakrishna was seized with an irresistible desire to learn the truth of the Christian religion. He began to listen to readings from the Bible, by Sambhu Charan Mallick, a gentleman of Calcutta and a devotee of the Master. Sri Ramakrishna became fascinated by the life and teachings of Jesus. One day he was seated in the parlour of Jadu Mallick's garden house (This expression is used throughout to translate the Bengali word denoting a rich man's country house set in a garden.) at Dakshineswar, when his eyes became fixed on a painting of the Madonna and Child. Intently watching it, he became gradually overwhelmed with divine emotion. The figures in the picture took on life, and the rays of light emanating from them entered his soul. The effect of this experience was stronger than that of the vision of Mohammed. In dismay he cried out, "O Mother! What are You doing to me?" And, breaking through the barriers of creed and religion, he entered a new realm of ecstasy. Christ possessed his soul. For three days he did not set foot in the Kali temple. On the fourth day, in the afternoon, as he was walking in the Panchavati, he saw coming toward him a person with beautiful large eyes, serene countenance, and fair skin. As the two faced each other, a voice rang out in the depths of Sri Ramakrishna's soul: "Behold the Christ, who shed His heart's blood for the redemption of the world, who suffered a sea of anguish for love of men. It is He, the Master Yogi, who is in eternal union with God. It is Jesus, Love Incarnate."

shortIntroduction.text: Born Manikarnika, Lakshmibai married Gangadhar Rao of Jhansi in 1842 and became its Rani; her political position came from this royal marriage.

shortIntroduction.text: Company intervention weakened princely rulers through residents, reduced revenues and territory, and disbanded forces; Lakshmibai’s dispute arose within this erosion of royal power.

contributions.text: NCERT dates Jhansi’s annexation under the Doctrine of Lapse to 1854, placing the succession dispute before the 1857 uprising.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: The doctrine declared that if an Indian ruler died without a male heir his kingdom would “lapse”, that is, become a part of Company territory. One kingdom after another was annexed simply by applying this doctrine: Satara (1848), Sambalpur (1850), Udaipur (1852), Nagpur (1853) and Jhansi (1854). Finally, in 1856, the Company also took over Awadh.

contributions.text: The Company denied recognition both to Jhansi’s adopted prince and to Lakshmibai as his regent, challenging her claim to political authority as well as the child’s succession.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: Rani Lakshmi Bai, the Queen of Jhansi, led her army against the British in 1857. The death of the king, Gangadhar Rao, had left the throne without a natural heir. The East India Company denied recognition to the adopted prince, or to the Queen as his regent and annexed the kingdom. Undeterred, Rani Lakshmi Bai took the reins of government, reorganised her forces and fought the colonialists. A figure of loss but not of defeat, the Rani lost her family, her kingdom and died in battle, but she also became a legendary figure in Indian history.

contemporaryRelevance.text: Deshpande analyzes how Lakshmibai became an icon of heroic Indian womanhood through later narratives, separating nationalist memory from direct evidence about 1857.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: This paper examines a concatenation of influential narratives of different genres that have become critical sources for a history of the rebel leader Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi and for configuring her as an icon of heroic Indian womanhood. contemporaryRelevance.text: Lakshmibai’s memory developed through late nineteenth-century Marathi writing and mid-twentieth-century Hindi narratives, rather than remaining a fixed image after her death.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: This paper examines a concatenation of influential narratives of different genres that have become critical sources for a history of the rebel leader Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi and for configuring her as an icon of heroic Indian womanhood. It places each of these sources, ranging from late nineteenth-century Marathi texts to mid-twentieth-century Hindi narratives, within their specific spatiotemporal setting and highlights the contradictory regional projects underlying apparently smooth nationalist narratives. Through a close examination of the making of the Lakshmibai archive, the author argues that a consideration of the editorial and textual practices that went into the making of reliable and usable archives for a modern historiography is critical to the unpacking of nationalist historiographies.

sourcingStandardViolationsWithheld.text: Singh shows that colonial depictions used sexualized judgments about Lakshmibai to explain or diminish a woman’s political and military opposition; gender affected the construction of her reputation.
In her letter dated about 12 June 1857, reproduced by Majumdar, Lakshmibai reported coercion and extortion by mutineers; this is her account, not independent proof of innocence.
The government’s July 1857 response made Erskine’s recognition conditional on Lakshmibai’s account proving true, revealing disagreement and suspicion within the British administration.
Singh finds that British literary portrayals alternated between demonizing Lakshmibai and admiring her as a worthy enemy; there was no single neutral British portrait.

Deshpande argues that seemingly unified nationalist stories about Lakshmibai conceal different regional projects and editorial choices; later biographies must be read in their own historical settings.

Rose’s siege dispatch blamed Jhansi’s inhabitants, including the Rani, for murder and plunder; this collective accusation must be read as an adversarial claim alongside her letters and later source criticism.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: Published in 1901, Michael White's novel Lachmi Bai Rani of Jhansi: The Jeanne D'Arc of India places the Rani within the structural imperatives of a hagiography by smoothing over her anti-colonial sentiments and comparing her to a European model of heroic and saintly womanhood, Joan of Arc. Victorian narratives oscillated between the Rani's characterisation as the sexually voracious and deranged architect of mayhem and her depiction as a worthy foe, the Indian rendition of Boadicea. Savitribai had also taken teacherís training at Ms.

lifeAndContext.text: Narake interprets Savitribai’s move from the household into public teaching as a significant change in women’s public life; the significance concerns access to authority and knowledge, not an unqualified claim that no woman taught before her.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: If these documents are to be given consideration, Savitribai Phule may well have been the first Indian woman teacher and headmistress. Her stepping across the threshold of the home to teach marks the beginning of the ëpublic lifeí of the modern Indian woman. In the deposition given by Jotirao to the Hunter Education Commission on 19th October 1882, making a note of his educational work, he said, ìThere was no school -- 11 of 54 -- 10 for girls that could be called ëindigenousí at that time here.

contemporaryRelevance.text: Azim Premji University retells Savitribai’s life through Patua-style illustrations, evidence of her later role as an educational exemplar; the dramatized scenes and dialogue are modern interpretation.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: In her own right, Savitribai was a woman ahead of her times, in thought and action, with the courage and sensitivity to lead a life defined by choices often ridiculed or aggressively opposed by society and its institutionalized ways. This graphic novel is an attempt to take the reader through Savitribai’s life, her ideas and thinking which shaped the very visible and impactful work she accomplished along with Jotirao. Obtaining an education after being married at the age of 9, Savitribai went on to become one of the first few women teachers in India. Together, the couple then started a school for girls (widely considered the first such school for girls) – a space of empowerment and equality, where no discrimination was allowed room and the running of which succeeded despite opposition from every quarter. These pathbreaking ventures were but the beginnings of further work driven by selfless devotion to service of the oppressed and destitute, and a vision of equality, fairness, and justice. They believed that education is the remedy for backward thinking and for creating equal opportunities. We decided to evoke the richness of Savitribai’s life and ideals through the folk art form of Patua from West Bengal, traditionally a storytelling form. The beautiful illustrations that make this graphic novel are from the hands of Sumon Chitrakar – a Patua artist from Midnapore.

contemporaryRelevance.text: During Pune’s plague outbreak in 1897, Savitribai worked with her physician son Yeshwant to provide treatment and bring patients to a hospital, according to Narake.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: The government took up the task of controlling the epidemic under the leadership of an officer called Rand. Savitribai asked Yeshwant to take leave and come back and made him set up a hospital on the fields of the Sasane family. She would herself pick up sick people and bring them to the hospital and treat them.

contemporaryRelevance.text: Her letter of 20 April 1877 describes Satyashodhak committees and relief squads distributing essential supplies during famine, evidence of organized social service as part of the reform movement.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: Some are eating poisonous fruits, and drinking their own urine to quench their thirst. They cry for food and drink, and then they die.Our Satyashodhak volunteers have formed committees to provide food and other life-saving material to the people in need. They have formed relief squads.Brother Kondaj and his wife Umabai are taking good care of me.

contemporaryRelevance.text: In the same 1877 letter, Savitribai reports negotiating with the Collector for detained volunteers and securing food aid, showing relief work involved dealing with colonial administrative power.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: I asked the Collector why the good volunteers had been framed with false charges and arrested without any rhyme or reason. I asked him to release them immediately. The Collector was quite decent and unbiased.

Descriptions of the Phules as pioneers must be qualified: Narake’s history mentions an existing missionary girls’ school at Ahmednagar, so “India’s first girls’ school” should not be read as a literal claim that all girls’ schooling began with them.

Later biographical accounts describe Savitribai carrying a spare sari after hostile people threw filth at her on the way to school; the anecdote illustrates remembered harassment but is not presented as a directly verified eyewitness record.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: In her own right, Savitribai was a woman ahead of her times, in thought and action, with the courage and sensitivity to lead a life defined by choices often ridiculed or aggressively opposed by society and its institutionalized ways. Obtaining an education after being married at the age of 9, Savitribai went on to become one of the first few women teachers in India. Together, the couple then started a school for girls (widely considered the first such school for girls) – a space of empowerment and equality, where no discrimination was allowed room and the running of which succeeded despite opposition from every quarter. We decided to evoke the richness of Savitribai’s life and ideals through the folk art form of Patua from West Bengal, traditionally a storytelling form. contributions.text: As a student, Ramanujan studied G. S. Carr's compendium of mathematical results, an important resource for his independent mathematical learning.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: It was in the Town High School that Ramanujan came across a mathematics book by G S Carr called Synopsis of elementary results in pure mathematics. This book, with its very concise style, allowed Ramanujan to teach himself mathematics, but the style of the book was to have a rather unfortunate effect on the way Ramanujan was later to write down mathematics since it provided the only model that he had of written mathematical arguments.

contributions.text: Hardy and Ramanujan developed an asymptotic formula for the partition function p(n).

citations.evidenceExcerpt: These papers by Ramanujan on partitions were followed by a joint paper with Hardy on the asymptotic value of p(n). Their result was remarkable, since not only did their formula give good approximations to the values already calculated but also seemed to give an exact expression for p(n); Rademacher later established that this was correct.

challenges.text: Ramanujan became seriously ill in 1917 and spent much of his remaining time in England in sanatoria.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: Sadly, in the spring of 1917 Ramanujan fell ill, and was in and out of sanatoria for the rest of his stay in Cambridge. By early 1919 Ramanujan seemed to have recovered sufficiently, and decided to travel back to India.

challenges.text: Ramanujan lost his Government College scholarship after concentrating on mathematics and neglecting other subjects.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: However, the following year his scholarship was not renewed because Ramanujan devoted more and more of his time to mathematics and neglected his other subjects.

challenges.text: Ramanujan supported himself as a clerk at the Madras Port Trust while continuing mathematical research.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: In 1912 Ramanujan applied for the post of clerk in the accounts section of the Madras Port Trust. In his letter of application he wrote [3]:- I have passed the Matriculation Examination and studied up to the First Arts but was prevented from pursuing my studies further owing to several untoward circumstances.

challenges.text: Without a university mathematics education or regular access to current research, Ramanujan continued developing ideas independently.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: In the following years he worked on mathematics developing his own ideas without any help and without any real idea of the then current research topics other than that provided by Carr's book.

leadershipRelationalCharacteristics.text: Hardy's encouraging reply led to a sustained exchange of letters with Ramanujan.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: So Hardy sent an encouraging reply to Ramanujan, which led to a frequent exchange of letters. It was clear to Hardy that Ramanujan was totally exceptional: however, in spite of his amazing feats in mathematics, he lacked the basic tools of the trade of a professional mathematician.

leadershipRelationalCharacteristics.text: Ramanujan entered Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1914 and developed his work with Hardy and Littlewood's guidance.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: Very favorable fellowship arrangements were made, and Ramanujan was admitted to Trinity College in 1914. He developed rapidly under the guidance of Hardy and Littlewood, who also helped him to publish his papers in English periodicals.

leadershipRelationalCharacteristics.text: Ramanujan sent Hardy a long list of mathematical discoveries in 1913, beginning the correspondence that changed his research opportunities.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: So, at the beginning of 1913, when he was just past 25, he dispatched a letter to Hardy in Cambridge with a long list of his discoveries –- a letter which changed both their lives. Although only 36 when he received Ramanujan’s letter, Hardy was already the leading mathematician in England.

leadershipRelationalCharacteristics.text: The University of Madras awarded Ramanujan a two-year scholarship in 1913, enabling him to pursue research.

citations.evidenceExcerpt: Indeed the University of Madras did give Ramanujan a scholarship in May 1913 for two years and, in 1914, Hardy brought Ramanujan to Trinity College, Cambridge, to begin an extraordinary collaboration.

contemporaryRelevance.text: The Royal Society describes work on proving and understanding Ramanujan's recorded equations as an ongoing part of his mathematical legacy.

sourcingStandardViolationsWithheld.text: Bose’s Axis alliances cannot be separated from the anti-colonial goal he claimed, but neither can they be treated as morally or politically uncomplicated; historians examine both agency and dependence.
Japanese archival scholarship cautions against portraying Japan simply as a disinterested liberator: Japanese leaders treated Indian nationalism as useful to their own strategic project.
The INA trials strengthened nationalist politics, but historians debate how much they contributed relative to postwar exhaustion, Indian mass politics, military unrest and wider imperial change.
British archival cataloguing documents that colonial officials maintained a file on Bose’s reported death at Taihoku; a catalogue entry alone cannot resolve the cause, witnesses or remains.
The National Archives of India holds large declassified INA and Bose-related collections, enabling continued research rather than licensing simple claims that every archival question is closed.
Government archival releases include material from the Khosla and Mukherjee inquiries, showing that Bose’s disappearance has been repeatedly investigated by Indian institutions.

The Mukherjee Commission revisited the reported 18 August 1945 Taihoku crash and sought additional records, so accounts of Bose’s death should distinguish evidence, inquiry conclusions and later claims.

The death controversy requires separate appraisal of Japanese witness material, British colonial records, Indian inquiries, Soviet-related allegations and later public memory; no single source family decides every question.
The 1956 Shah Nawaz Committee concluded that Bose died in an air crash and that the Renkoji ashes were his; this is an official finding, not the end of disagreement.

Sarga 
That night in Ayodhya passed over with agony. At sunrise the Brahmins who enthrone a 
person as a king, assembled and requested Vasista the family priest of Ikshvakus to select a youth to 
be crowned as a king of Ayodhya. They enunciated the various evil consequences of allowing the country 
without a king and leaving it in anarchy.
----
That night in Ayodhya, which was joyless in a weeping tone and thronged with people with 
tears in their throats, slowly passed over. At sunrise, when the night had passed over, the Brahmins 
who place a king on the throne, together gathered at the assembly.
Markandeya, Moudgalya, Vamadeva, Kasyapa,Katyayana, Goutama and the greatly famous Jabali-all 
these Brahmans together with the ministers turned towards the excellent royal priest Vasishta and one 
by one spoke as follows: "King Dasaratha having obtained death due to grief born of separation from 
his sons (Rama and Lakshmana), the night which burdened like a hundred years, has passed over with great 
difficulty. The monarch has gone to heaven. Rama took retreat in a forest. The brilliant Lakshmana followed 
suit and went along with Rama. Both Bharata and Satrughna, the annihilator of enemies, are encamped 
in the beautiful house of their maternal uncle in the city of Rajagriha in the kingdom of Kekaya. Hence, 
let anyone here in Ikshvaku dynasty be made a king today itself lest our nation without a king should 
result in a collapse indeed. Lightning clouds in the sky with a great noise of thunder, will not yield 
rain on the land in a country without a king. Even a fist of seeds are not disbursed in a ruler-less 
land. In anarchy, even a son is not amenable to the control of a father nor a wife in the authority 
of her husband. In a ruler-less land, there is no wealth. Where there is no king, there is no (faithful) 
wife. Another very dangerous thing is there. In a ruler less territory, how can there be truth? In a 
ruler-less country, people do not cause to make a delightful assembly nor erect beautiful parks or temples. 
In a ruler-less territory, those who frequently perform sacrificial rites, those who have self-restraint, 
those who firmly adhere to a vow as well as Brahmins do not carry out Soma sacrifices. In a ruler-less 
land, Brahmans who obtained wealth and sacrificers in great sacrificial rites do not bestow proper gifts. 
In such territory, festivals and gatherings exalting the kingdom in which actors, and dancers exhibit 
their talents are not frequently arranged. Litigants do not get their disputes settled and persons who 
have a knack for narrating stories do not gratify story- lovers with their tales. Girls adorned in gold 
do not go together to parks to play there in the evening. In a lord less land, lustful men do not go 
out to woods with ladies in speedily moving vehicles."
"In a lord less land, rich people living on agriculture and cattle rearing do not sleep 
in their abodes well protected, with their doors open. In a land without emperor, sixty year old elephants 
with bells tied around their tusks, do not roam around on royal high ways. In a ruler less land, the 
noise of plucking the bow string with the palm, produced by archers continuously discharging arrows 
while practicing the use of their bows, is not heard. Where, traders who go to distant places, carrying 
with them several merchandises, cannot travel safely in their voyages. A monk who wanders alone, who

Introduction
 Vashishta offers hospitality to Vishvamitra and his armies. Even though the King Vishvamitra is 
 disinclined to pressurise a hermit with such a burdensome affair of hospitality to hosts, Vashishta 
 entreats the king to accept. Vishvamitra had to oblige the same. Vashishta summons his do-all Divine 
 Sacred Cow, Shabala, also known as Kaamadhenu, requests her to generate heaps of tasteful foodstuffs 
 for a royal banquet as well as for military rations.

Valmiki Ramayana - Ayodhya Kanda in Prose
Sarga 
That night in Ayodhya passed over with agony. At sunrise the Brahmins who enthrone a 
person as a king, assembled and requested Vasista the family priest of Ikshvakus to select a youth to 
be crowned as a king of Ayodhya. They enunciated the various evil consequences of allowing the country 
without a king and leaving it in anarchy.
----
That night in Ayodhya, which was joyless in a weeping tone and thronged with people with 
tears in their throats, slowly passed over. At sunrise, when the night had passed over, the Brahmins 
who place a king on the throne, together gathered at the assembly.
Markandeya, Moudgalya, Vamadeva, Kasyapa,Katyayana, Goutama and the greatly famous Jabali-all 
these Brahmans together with the ministers turned towards the excellent royal priest Vasishta and one 
by one spoke as follows: "King Dasaratha having obtained death due to grief born of separation from 
his sons (Rama and Lakshmana), the night which burdened like a hundred years, has passed over with great 
difficulty. The monarch has gone to heaven. Rama took retreat in a forest. The brilliant Lakshmana followed 
suit and went along with Rama. Both Bharata and Satrughna, the annihilator of enemies, are encamped 
in the beautiful house of their maternal uncle in the city of Rajagriha in the kingdom of Kekaya. Hence, 
let anyone here in Ikshvaku dynasty be made a king today itself lest our nation without a king should 
result in a collapse indeed. Lightning clouds in the sky with a great noise of thunder, will not yield 
rain on the land in a country without a king. Even a fist of seeds are not disbursed in a ruler-less 
land. In anarchy, even a son is not amenable to the control of a father nor a wife in the authority 
of her husband. In a ruler-less land, there is no wealth. Where there is no king, there is no (faithful) 
wife. Another very dangerous thing is there. In a ruler less territory, how can there be truth? In a 
ruler-less country, people do not cause to make a delightful assembly nor erect beautiful parks or temples. 
In a ruler-less territory, those who frequently perform sacrificial rites, those who have self-restraint, 
those who firmly adhere to a vow as well as Brahmins do not carry out Soma sacrifices. In a ruler-less 
land, Brahmans who obtained wealth and sacrificers in great sacrificial rites do not bestow proper gifts. 
In such territory, festivals and gatherings exalting the kingdom in which actors, and dancers exhibit 
their talents are not frequently arranged. Litigants do not get their disputes settled and persons who 
have a knack for narrating stories do not gratify story- lovers with their tales. Girls adorned in gold 
do not go together to parks to play there in the evening. In a lord less land, lustful men do not go 
out to woods with ladies in speedily moving vehicles."
"In a lord less land, rich people living on agriculture and cattle rearing do not sleep 
in their abodes well protected, with their doors open. In a land without emperor, sixty year old elephants 
with bells tied around their tusks, do not roam around on royal high ways. In a ruler less land, the 
noise of plucking the bow string with the palm, produced by archers continuously discharging arrows 
while practicing the use of their bows, is not heard. Where, traders who go to distant places, carrying 
with them several merchandises, cannot travel safely in their voyages. A monk who wanders alone, who 
has subdued his senses, who mediates himself on the soul and who takes up an abode wherever evening

Introduction
 Vashishta offers hospitality to Vishvamitra and his armies. Even though the King Vishvamitra is 
 disinclined to pressurise a hermit with such a burdensome affair of hospitality to hosts, Vashishta 
 entreats the king to accept. Vishvamitra had to oblige the same. Vashishta summons his do-all Divine 
 Sacred Cow, Shabala, also known as Kaamadhenu, requests her to generate heaps of tasteful foodstuffs 
 for a royal banquet as well as for military rations.

on seeing; paramapriitaH = is highly rejoiced; vinayaat praNataH = obediently, made 
an obeisance.
On seeing at that best sage among best meditators Sage Vashishta, the great-mighty and valorous Vishvamitra 
is highly rejoiced and obediently made an obeisance to the sage. [1-52-1]

Introduction
Vashishta nullifies Vishvamitra's missiles just by his Brahma's baton. All missiles 
are defused when Vashishta consumed tghem. Vishvamitra launches the highest missile, 
namely Brahma-missile, which too is consumed by Vashishta, whereby the body of Vashishta 
becomes a Brahma missile and starts to emit radiation. Then, upon the prayer of 
gods and saints, Vashishta withdraws the effect of that missile. Vishvamitra on 
seeing this concludes that mere missiles are of no use and thus he embarks on a 
sublime ascesis for Brahma-hood.
Verse Locator
evam ukto vasiShThena vishvaamitro mahaabalaH |
aagneyam as.htram utkShipya tiShTha tiShTha iti ca abraviit || 1-56-1
1. mahaabalaH vishvaamitraH = great-mighty, Vishvamitra; vasiSThena 
evam uktaH = by Vashishta, this way, spoken to; aagneyam astram utkSipya 
= fiery, missile, brandishing; tiSTha tiSTha = withstand, withstand [this 
missile]; iti abraviit ca = thus, said [challenged,] also.
"When Vashishta spoke in this way, the great-mighty Vishvamitra brandishing Fiery-missile 
challenged Vashishta saying, 'withstand this, withstand this..." Thus, sage Shataananda 
continued his narration of Vishvamitra's legend. [1-56-1]
Verse Locator
brahmadaNDam samudyaMya kaala daNDam iva aparam |
vasiShTho bhagavaan krodhaat idam vacanam abraviit || 1-56-2
2. bhagavaan vasiSThaH = reverential one, Vashishta; aparam kaala daNDam 
iva = the other, Terminator's, baton, like; brahma daNDam sam udyamya 
= Brahma's, baton, well, raising up; krodhaat idam vacanam abraviit = furiously, 
this, sentence, spoke.
"That reverential sage Vashishta then upraising his Brahma-baton, which is like 
the other baton of the Terminator, spoke this sentence furiously. [1-56-2]
Verse Locator
kshatra bandho sthito asmi eSha yad balam tad vidarshaya |
naashayaami adya te darpam shas.htrasya tava gaadhija || 1-56-3
3. kshatra bandhaH = oh, Kshatriya, meritless; eSa = this me;
sthitaH asmi = staying, I am; yat balam = which, prowess - you 
have; tat vi darshaya = that, entirely, you display; gaadhi ja 
= oh, to Gaadhi, one born to - Vishvamitra; adya te darpam = now, your, 
vanity; tava shastrasya [darpam] = your, missile's, [vanity]; naashayaami 
= I will ruin.
" 'I am staying here only, you meritless Kshatriya, you may clearly display whatever 
prowess you have, oh, Gaadhi's son Vishvamitra, I will now ruin whatever vanity 
you or your missiles have. [1-56-3]
Verse Locator
kva ca te kShatriya balam kva ca brahma balam mahat |
pashya brahma balam divyam mama kshatriya paaMsana || 1-56-4
4. kshatriya paansana = oh, Kshatriya, abased one; te kSatriya balam 
kva = your, Kshatriya's force [force of belligerence's,] where is; mahat 
brahma balam kva ca = supreme, Brahma's [sagacity's,] force, where is; 
mama divyam brahma balam pashya = my, seraphic, Brahma's [sagacity's,] strength, 
you watch.
" 'Where stands the force of belligerence when compared to the supreme force of 
sagacity, you abased Kshatriya, watch out for my strength of seraphic sagacity." 
So said Vashishta to Vishvamitra. [1-56-4]
Verse Locator
tasya as.htram gaadhi putrasya ghoram aagneyam uttamam |
brahma daNDena tat shaaMtam agneH vega iva aMbhasaa || 1-56-5
5. tasya gaadhi putrasya = his, Gaadhi, son's; uttamam ghoram tat aagneyam 
astram = matchless, deadly, that, Fire, missile; [udyatam = projected, 
bolted]; ambhasaa agneH vega iva = by water, fire's, speed [rage,] as [silenced] 
with; brahma daNDena shaantam = by Brahma's, baton [of Vashishta,] that, 
is silenced.
"With his baton of Brahma Vashishta silenced that matchless and deadly Fiery-missile 
of Gaadhi's son, namely Vishvamitra, as a deluge of water silencing a rage of fire. 
[1-56-5]

Introduction
Vashishta urges Rama to grant the prayer of Bharata. Rama replies that the command given by his father cannot be disregarded. Bharata
then decides to undertake a fest unto death as a last resort to exert pressure on Rama. On Rama's dubbing such a step as repugnant to the code of
conduct prescribed for a kshatriya, Bharata requests Rama to allow him to remain in the forest as the latter's proxy. Rama, however, rules out this
proposition also, saying that it is a matter of reproach. He reaffirms his resolve to enter Ayodhya only after implementing the pledge given to his
father.
